lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: Ajax. You went out of your mind, killed yourself, and came within a hair of killing the rest of us in the process. So what exactly do you have against Odysseus? The other day, when he came down to consult the oracle, you wouldn't even look at him — wouldn't give him the time of day, a fellow soldier, a comrade — just swept past him with that magnificent contemptuous stride of yours.
lines.note: Agamemnon opens as the weary mediator: not unsympathetic to Ajax, but committed to institutional reason. 'Magnificent contemptuous stride' renders ὑπεροπτικῶς μεγάλα βαίνων with a touch of irony.

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: And why wouldn't I? He's the reason I went mad in the first place. He was the only one who actually stood against me for the armour.
lines.note: Short, flat, unanswerable. Ajax is not performing grievance — he genuinely sees this as self-evident.

lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: Were you expecting to be the only one in the running? To walk off with the prize without even a contest?
lines.note: Dry, not cruel. Agamemnon is doing the institutional voice — 'you can't win if no one is allowed to compete.'

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: For that particular prize, yes. The armour belonged to my cousin. It should have come to me — that's family. And you lot, the rest of you, better men than Odysseus by a considerable margin, you all stood down and let me have it. It was the son of Laertes — a man I personally saved from being cut to pieces by the Trojans on more than one occasion — who decided he deserved it. That he was the more suitable candidate.
lines.note: The bitterness here is real, but Ajax is making a legal argument, not a sentimental one. 'Son of Laertes' — he won't use the name.

lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: Then blame Thetis, Ajax — that's where your grievance belongs. The armour was hers to pass on to you, her kinsman, and instead she threw it open to general competition.
lines.note: Agamemnon is trying to redirect. This is the mediated compromise position.

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: No. I blame Odysseus. He's the one who put his hand up.
lines.note: [pause] Two sentences. He's done with the argument; this is the verdict.

lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: Ajax, he's a man — he reached for glory. We all did. Every one of us ran risks for exactly the same reason, and the fact is, he beat you — in front of Trojan judges, no less.
lines.note: Agamemnon presses the institutional logic to its conclusion. 'In front of Trojan judges' is the twist of the knife he probably shouldn't deliver.

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: I know who gave the verdict against me. [pause] I won't say anything about the gods. But hate Odysseus? I couldn't stop even if Athena herself ordered me to.
lines.note: The restraint on the gods makes the final line land harder. Ajax's grievance is principled, permanent, and entirely unsolvable — which is the point. He is the one figure in the underworld who has not made his peace.
